questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Two Dimensions
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F=({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,i-({e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,j.$ 
Evaluate $∇\cdot F$ at the point $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
∇\cdot F=\text{div}\,F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡y) \\  & ={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y-{e}^{x}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡y). \\  & =2{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point  $(0,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(0,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =2{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =2\cdot 1\cdot 1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F=(2x+3y-4z)^{2}\,i+(2x+3y-4z)^{2}\,j+(2x+3y-4z)^{2}\,k.$ 
Find $∇\cdot F.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
∇\cdot F=\text{div}\,F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((2x+3y-4z)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((2x+3y-4z)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}((2x+3y-4z)^{2}) \\  & =4(2x+3y-4z)+6(2x+3y-4z)-8(2x+3y-4z) \\  & =2(2x+3y-4z) \\  & =4x+6y-8z.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F=x(y{e}^{z}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,i+xy{e}^{z}\,j+z(x+1)\,k.$ 
Evaluate $∇\cdot F$ at the point $(1,1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x(y{e}^{z}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y))+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy{e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z(x+1)) \\  & =(y{e}^{z}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y)+x{e}^{z}+(x+1) \\  & =y{e}^{z}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y+x{e}^{z}+x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(1,1,0),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(1,1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{0}+\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1\cdot {e}^{0}+1+1 \\  & =1+0+1+1+1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F=xz\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,i+y{x}^{2}\,j+x{z}^{2}{e}^{y}\,k.$ 
Evaluate $∇\cdot F$ at the point $(1,0,-2).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xz\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{x}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{z}^{2}{e}^{y}) \\  & =z\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{x}^{2}+2xz{e}^{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(1,0,-2),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(1,0,-2) & =(-2)\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0+{1}^{2}+2\cdot 1\cdot (-2)\cdot {e}^{0} \\  & =-2+1-4 \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044029/assets/33f0353e3856fb2b458d17ed1959918e6a3dd96fd0a966d971575ffc212402f0.png)

Consider the vector field $F$ shown above. Which of the following statements are true everywhere in the domain of $F?$

- $\text{div}\,F=0$
- $\text{div}\,F>0$
- $\text{div}\,F<0$
- $F$ is solenoidal
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14044029/assets/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement II is true, whereas statements I and III are false. Notice that the lengths of the vectors increase as we move horizontally and vertically away from the origin. Therefore, the vector field $F$ acts like a source at every point.

- Statement IV is false. Since $∇\cdot F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Divergence of a Vector Field in Two Dimensions
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=\ln(2x+y)\,\mathbf{i}+ x^2e^{3y}\,\mathbf{j}.$ 
Evaluate $\nabla \cdot\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,0).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j}$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+y))+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{e}^{3y}) \\  & =\frac{2}{2x+y}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{3y}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf {F}$ at the point $(1,0),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(∇\cdot F)(1,0) & =\frac{2}{2(1)+0}+3(1)^{2}{e}^{3(0)} \\  & =1+3 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}=(2x-y)^2\,\mathbf{i}+(3y-2z)^2\,\mathbf{j}+(x-2z)^2\,\mathbf{k}.$ Evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf{F}$ at the point $(1,2,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $\mathbf{F}=P\,\mathbf{i}+Q\,\mathbf{j} + R\,\mathbf k$ is a vector field on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $\mathbf F$ all exist, then the divergence of $\mathbf F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\textrm{div}\,\mathbf F = \nabla\cdot\mathbf{F}=\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial x}+\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial y}+\dfrac{\partial R}{\partial z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((2x-y)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((3y-2z)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}((x-2z)^{2}) \\  & =4(2x-y)+6(3y-2z)-4(x-2z) \\  & =4x+14y-4z.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\textrm{div}\,\mathbf { F}$ at the point $(1,2,1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F(1,2,1) & =4(1)+14(2)-4(1) \\  & =28.\end{aligned}
$$
